summary: Six lines from the great acrostic on God’s instruction reject the way of falsehood and prize the Torah above wealth.

context.title: Six verses from the Torah psalm
paragraphs: Psalm 119 is an alphabetic acrostic of twenty-two stanzas, one for each Hebrew letter, and every verse of a stanza begins with that letter. [c1] The six verses here come from five of them: Daleth, Teth, Lamed, Mem (two verses) and Shin. [c2] Jamieson, Fausset and Brown suggest that the artful form served teaching and memory. [c3]

By one older count, only two verses in the whole psalm lack some term for God’s word. [c4] Torah, usually rendered law, is one of those terms and appears three times in these six verses. [c5] The psalm is tied to no particular event; it is the prayer of someone who has set God’s declared will before him as the rule of his life. [c6]

Three of the six verses name šeqer, falsehood, as the way the psalmist rejects. [c7] Older commentators took this less as the habit of telling lies than as any conduct not governed by God’s truth. [c8] Against it stands a word fixed for ever in the heavens, which the psalmist values above any amount of earthly riches. [c9]

translationNotes.summary: Tôrâ means direction or instruction before it means law in a legal sense.
translationNotes.body: The lexicon gives direction and instruction as the senses of tôrâ, alongside law. [c10] Proverbs uses the same noun for a mother’s teaching and a sage’s. [c11] Jamieson, Fausset and Brown call it a term of general purport denoting instruction. [c12] Delitzsch notes that in v. 29 it means living instruction rather than a rigid fixed teaching. [c13]

translationNotes.summary: The verb asks for grace: the psalmist receives God’s instruction as a favour, not as something owed.
translationNotes.body: Ḥānan means to show favour or be gracious. [c14] It is the verb of the priestly blessing in Num 6:25. [c15] Here it takes two objects, so the psalmist asks God to be gracious to him with the law itself, and Barnes stresses that he does not claim it as a right. [c16] Ellicott calls this plea for grace the persistent cry of the psalm. [c17]

translationNotes.summary: Niṣṣāb pictures something set up and standing, like a pillar planted in heaven.
translationNotes.body: The verb means to take one’s stand, or to stand where one is stationed. [c18] Barnes links it with setting up a pillar, an altar or a monument. [c19] The Cambridge Bible renders it standeth fast and reads the verse as a single clause, with the Greek, the Targum and Jerome. [c20] Delitzsch draws the conclusion that God’s word, standing in heaven, shares heaven’s stability. [c21]

translationNotes.summary: Šeqer is deception that disappoints: in this psalm, a way of life false to God rather than a single lie.
translationNotes.body: Šeqer covers deception, fraud and false testimony, and first of all whatever deceives, disappoints and betrays. [c22] The Pulpit Commentary holds that in this verse the psalmist is not speaking of the habit of lying. [c23] The Cambridge Bible hears instead the pull of heathen ways against the truth of God’s law. [c24] Its opposite, in verse 30, is the way of faithfulness and loyalty to God. [c25]

claims.text: Psalm 119 is divided into twenty-two stanzas named after the letters of the Hebrew alphabet; each stanza has eight verses beginning with its letter.
Ps 119:29, 72, 89, 101, 104 and 163 begin with the letters Daleth, Teth, Lamed, Mem, Mem and Shin, in the stanzas Keil and Delitzsch call the eightfold Daleth, Teth, Lamed, Mem and Shin.
Jamieson, Fausset and Brown suggest the psalm was meant for instruction, especially of the young, and that its artificial structure aided memory.
By the count of Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, only two verses of Psalm 119 (vv. 122 and 132) contain no term for God’s word.
The noun תּוֹרָה occurs in Ps 119:29, 72 and 163.
Psalm 119 is not tied to a special occasion, and the psalmist has set God’s declared will before himself as the rule of his life.
The noun שֶׁקֶר occurs in Ps 119:29, 104 and 163.
Commentators take the falsehood of these verses as conduct not governed by God’s truth rather than the habit of lying.
Ps 119:89 says God’s word stands for ever in heaven, and Ps 119:72 values God’s law above great quantities of gold and silver, that is, above any amount of riches.
תּוֹרָה means direction, instruction, law.
In Proverbs תּוֹרָה is used of a mother’s instruction (Prv 1:8) and of the teaching of sages (Prv 13:14).
Jamieson, Fausset and Brown describe law in Psalm 119 as a term of general purport denoting the instruction of God’s word.
Keil and Delitzsch note that in Ps 119:29 תּוֹרָה has not the rigid notion of a fixed teaching but of living instruction.
The verb חָנַן means to show favour, to be gracious.
The priestly blessing in Num 6:25 uses the same verb חָנַן.
In Ps 119:29 חָנַן takes a double accusative, and the psalmist asks for the law as a favour, not as a right.
Ellicott renders the plea as be gracious to me according to thy law and calls it the persistent cry of the psalm.
The Niphal of נָצַב means to take one’s stand, stand, or be stationed.
Barnes notes that the word means to set up or cause to stand, as a column, an altar or a monument.
The Cambridge Bible renders the verb standeth fast and, following the Septuagint, the Targum and Jerome, treats Ps 119:89 as one clause.
Keil and Delitzsch say God’s word has heaven as its standing-place and therefore shares heaven-like stability.
שֶׁקֶר means deception, disappointment, falsehood, first of all what deceives, disappoints and betrays one.
The Pulpit Commentary holds that in Ps 119:163 the psalmist is not speaking of the habit of lying but of false religion or moral teaching.
The Cambridge Bible takes the falsehood of Ps 119:163 as heathenism and heathenish tendencies, in contrast to the truth of God’s law.
The way of falsehood in Ps 119:29 is contrasted with the way of faithfulness, of loyalty to God, in Ps 119:30.
